RT by @lookner: #Hurricane #LALA was the first hurricane to directly impact the Hawaiian Islands since INIKI in 1992, & it's left behind a trail of devastation. The most hurricane-prone US states are all very flat. #Hawaii—especially the Big Island—is *extremely* mountainous. And those mountains create special issues—and special weirdness! * EXTREME RAINFALL & ROCKSLIDES. The mountains amplified the rainfall on the E side & S end of the Big Island, with some places getting almost 3 ft of rain. And in some places, these rains unleashed catastrophic flooding & rockslides. * ELEVATION-ENHANCED WINDS. Higher elevations tend to get stronger winds in a hurricane, and this is an issue for Hawai'i, which has lots of residential neighborhoods thousands of feet above sea-level. These communities were hammered by damaging winds—even in locations far, far outside the hurricane's core. I've chased hurricanes in mountainous places before (Mexico, Taiwan, Jamaica, etc.), & this is some of the most stark elevation enhancement I've seen. For example, in beachside neighborhoods of Kona (where I'm staying), barely a twig or leaf was out of place after the storm, whereas neighborhoods in the nearby hills had wind damage. Hurricane-force gusts were measured in many places across the islands, with Mauna Kea summit (at over 13K ft) measuring a gust to a whopping 122 knots. * SNOW. Yep. On Mauna Kea Summit, it snowed. A total meteorological freak show. One last thing: There's a prevailing belief that the mountain peaks on the Big Island will always weaken approaching storms. LALA violated that belief. It did the exact opposite—strengthening into a hurricane as it neared the island.

Rents rose 31% year-on-year in March, while Iranian media reported housing prices in Tehran about 50% higher than a year earlier. The dollar value of Iran’s minimum wage has also fallen from about $105 to $86 since late March, Reuters reported. The US naval blockade has added to economic pressure by disrupting trade and effectively cutting off gasoline imports, Iranian lawmaker Reza Sepahvand told ILNA on Saturday. Iran is producing about 130 million liters of gasoline a day against consumption of 137 million liters.
